Disease Outbreak Disrupts Panama’s Transportation and Logistics Sector

PANAMA CITY, June 14—A surge in dengue fever cases among workers in Panama’s transportation and logistics industry is disrupting cargo shipments and operations at several key logistics hubs, officials said Friday.

The outbreak, concentrated in the Colón Free Zone and the Pacific-side logistics corridor, has led to staff shortages and delays in cargo handling, according to the Panamanian Association of Logistics Operators (APLO). “Up to 18 percent of our workforce in critical areas is currently out sick or quarantined,” said APLO president Ricardo Mendoza. “This is impacting the efficiency of container processing and customs procedures.”

Authorities estimate that daily cargo volumes through major terminals have dropped by 12 percent since the beginning of June, with some warehouses operating on skeleton staff. The Ministry of Health reported 247 confirmed dengue cases among logistics workers in the last two weeks, attributing the spike to recent heavy rains and standing water near work sites, which have increased mosquito breeding.

“Teams are being stretched thin, and some dock operations are running at half capacity,” said Mariela Torres, spokesperson for AGT Logistics, one of the firms affected. “We are prioritizing essential shipments, but delays are unavoidable.”

The National Customs Authority has deployed additional inspectors to high-traffic areas to mitigate bottlenecks, but exporters report increasing wait times. “We’re seeing transit times rise by up to 48 hours for certain containers,” said Jorge Villalobos, an independent freight analyst. “If the outbreak continues, there could be longer-term impacts on supply chains through the Canal corridor.”

Trade unions have called for intensified fumigation campaigns and expanded healthcare support at logistics sites. Health officials said mobile clinics and mosquito control teams have been dispatched, but warned that the outbreak remains ongoing.
